title: That One Time I Found a Snake and Discovered Life Isn’t Fair September 23, 2026
author: Timothy Paul Jones
source: The Apologetics Newsletter by Timothy Paul Jones (timothypauljones.substack.com),
summary: Timothy Paul Jones, writing as a father of four, uses a comic boyhood memoir to illustrate a line from William Goldman’s novel The Princess Bride that he recommends repeating to children: life isn’t fair, it’s just fairer than death. He recounts being an eight-year-old at a fundamentalist Baptist school, exiled to the permanent distant outfield of the daily kickball game, who found a lawnmower-killed black rat snake and decided to share it by dropping it down a classmate’s dress. The humour comes from the boy’s rule-lawyering logic, cataloguing the dancing, angry outbursts and theft committed by everyone else under the school’s rule book while he alone ended up in detention. The move of the piece is to turn this childish sense of injustice into a lesson that keeping the rules and planning well do not guarantee that life turns out as expected. A closing disclaimer steps back into the adult and parental voice, acknowledging that dropping snakes down people’s backs is wrong and honouring the stern but kind teacher involved.
points: Jones offers The Princess Bride line "Life isn’t fair; it’s just fairer than death" as something worth repeating to your children.
The story gently satirises a school rule book obsessed with haircuts, rock music and pushed-in chairs while silent on what mattered.
His eight-year-old self tallies everyone else’s rule violations and cannot see why he is the one punished, a portrait of a boy’s moral reasoning.
The lesson he draws is that keeping every rule and planning well does not guarantee life will turn out the way you expected.
quotes: It’s a wonderful line to repeat to your children, though I do warn you that they’re likely to do some eye-rolling behind your back if you say it very often.

Not a live one, mind you. This one was mostly headless and appeared to have been an unwitting victim of the swirling blades of the school’s lawnmower. Still, seen through the eyes of an eight-year-old boy, it was a treasure.
To this day, I am very good at teamwork and school spirit as long as I don’t have to practice them with actual people.

The school’s rules described in detail how true Christians tapered their haircuts if they were men, avoided rock music and dancing, and always pushed in their chairs—presumably because tapered haircuts, beat-less music, and well-arranged chairs were such vital parts of Jesus’ earthly ministry.

I had kept every rule in the school’s manual and still, somehow, left the principal’s office with a detention slip in my hand. I realized then and there that keeping the rules and planning well does not guarantee everything in my life will turn out the way I thought it would.

As an adult and a father of four girls, yes, I do recognize that dropping snakes down people’s backs is not something that one ought to do, and I do sincerely hope that Rachel was not traumatized by these events.
